cases.name: built-in worked example
stdout: (no config - demo: Example Co., a fictional company, with invented numbers)
COHORT RETENTION CURVES - Example Co., customers by signup month
12 cohorts, 11 months of history, customer retention
RESULT: Retention levels off at about 40% from month 5
KEY FIGURES
Month 1 retention:               75%   95% band 72% to 77%
Month 9 retention:               38%   the last month at least 3 cohorts have reached
Months active, first 10:         5.3   of the first 10 months, the average customer was around for this many
CURVE (chained average, 95% band over the reliable months)
Month  Average   95% band        Cohorts
5    42.3%   39.7% to 44.9%        7   levels off from here
10    37.7%                         2   fewer than 3 cohorts
11    37.7%                         1   fewer than 3 cohorts
Levels off at about 40% from month 5 (the average of months 5 to 9, judged over 4 later months).
NEWER VS OLDER COHORTS, at month 6
Older 3 (2025-10 to 2025-12):         36.9%   pooled, 420 at start
Newer 3 (2026-01 to 2026-03):         40.8%   pooled, 490 at start
No clear difference between newer and older cohorts.
Difference +3.9 points (p = 0.228). Best cohort at month 6: 2026-03 (42%); weakest: 2025-10 (35%).
FINDINGS
[Note] Periods 10 to 11 come from fewer than 3 cohorts. They are drawn dashed and are not used to judge where the curve levels off.
AAJ'S VIEW
- In AAJ's view, a curve that levels off is a base to build on: from month 5 each month loses less than 2 points of the starting cohort, so what you acquire adds to a base that keeps.
- The levelling-off threshold (2 points per month), the 3-cohort minimum and the 2 later months it is judged over are tool rules, AAJ's choices, not benchmarks.
SOURCES
Curve: E. L. Kaplan and P. Meier, "Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations", Journal of the American Statistical Association 53 (1958).
95% band: M. Greenwood, "The natural duration of cancer", Reports on Public Health and Medical Subjects 33 (1926).

Newer vs older: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, "7.3.3. How can we determine whether two processes produce the same proportion of defectives?": https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section3/prc33.htm
p-value: M. Abramowitz and I. A. Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions, National Bureau of Standards (1964), formula 26.2.17.

stdout: COHORT RETENTION CURVES
5 cohorts, 5 quarters of history, revenue retention
RESULT: Retention has not levelled off yet
KEY FIGURES
Quarter 1 retention:            102%   the first drop is usually the biggest
Quarter 3 retention:            110%   the last quarter at least 3 cohorts have reached
Revenue over 4 quarters:        4.2x   multiples of the first quarter's revenue, per cohort
CURVE (chained average)
Quarter  Average   Cohorts
4   111.7%         2   fewer than 3 cohorts
5   112.6%         1   fewer than 3 cohorts
NEWER VS OLDER COHORTS, at quarter 2
Older 2 (Q1 2025 to Q2 2025):        109.2%   pooled, 92,000 at start
Newer 2 (Q3 2025 to Q4 2025):        105.1%   pooled, 99,000 at start
Newer cohorts look worse (no significance test for this data).
Difference -4.2 points. Best cohort at quarter 2: Q1 2025 (110%); weakest: Q3 2025 (103%).
FINDINGS
[Note] Periods 4 to 5 come from fewer than 3 cohorts. They are drawn dashed and are not used to judge where the curve levels off.

[Check] The curve has not levelled off within the data: it is still losing 2 points or more of the starting cohort per period. Retention that keeps falling means no cohort settles into a stable base yet, which puts a ceiling on growth however much you acquire.
[Note] Revenue in the average cohort ends above where it started: expansion outweighs churn and contraction over the first 3 periods.
AAJ'S VIEW
- The levelling-off threshold (2 points per quarter), the 3-cohort minimum and the 2 later quarters it is judged over are tool rules, AAJ's choices, not benchmarks.
SOURCES
Curve: E. L. Kaplan and P. Meier, "Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations", Journal of the American Statistical Association 53 (1958).
